### TAG-129: Example 12.19 Imperative form of expression

**Status:** 🟡 Partial

## Software Notes

**Root cause for TAG-129: **`res <= AB;` is nonsense output from a fallback path — meaning `writeContainedLookupTable` is rejecting OR entirely and falling through to something else. Tracing my own validation logic against OR's actual rows: I required every contained row's resolution to be `.fill` — but OR's rows (`0,0[0]`, `0,1[1]`, ...) are the bare "Constant Definition" abbreviated form, meaning their resolution is a single `.pure_value`, not a `.fill`. I conflated two genuinely different row shapes into one check:

* **Anonymous rows** (OR/AND/NOT, [TAG-137](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-137/example-1241-four-value-sequencer)'s fourstate) — each row is a bare literal/symbol, triggered by a *named *`.fill` in the outer resolution (`res<$A$B()>`), producing one table for that fill's destination.
* **Structured rows** ([TAG-136](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-136/example-1245-code-detector-state-machine)'s code detector) — each row has one or more *named* fills, triggered by a *bare *`.pure_value` in the outer resolution (no destination name at all), producing one table per destination the rows collectively cover.

My last patch only handled the structured shape, silently rejecting the anonymous one — which used to work before this change. That's a real regression on my part, now understood and fixable.

This is exactly the confirmation needed, and it resolves the open question cleanly — turns out this doesn't need call-graph tracing at all, it's purely positional.

**"Return a Content to Place of Invocation" confirms hypothesis #2 directly, in the book's own words: ***"The destination place $SUM in the destination list of the definition associates to the unnamed source place."* Walk it through [TAG-129](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-129/example-1219-imperative-form-of-expression) precisely: the invocation's output list is `(< > CARRYOUT < >)` — unnamed, then `CARRYOUT`. `FULLADD`'s own destinations are `($SUM $CARRY)` — in that same order. Position 0 (unnamed) corresponds to position 0 (`$SUM`); position 1 (`CARRYOUT`) corresponds to position 1 (`$CARRY`), which the book confirms matches for the named slot too. So the fix for the invocation-side case is exactly what I'd hoped but wasn't fully certain of last night: **when wiring an invocation's output, an unnamed slot borrows the name of the positionally-corresponding destination from the definition being invoked.** No tracing, no external context — purely mechanical.

**"Single Return to Place of Invocation" gives the definition-side case (§ empty-destination-list, like** `AND[(X<>Y<>)<> ]`) a clean, principled answer too. There's no destination to borrow from — by definition, this form *has* no destination list — so the natural, book-consistent move is: synthesize **one fixed, canonical output name** (e.g. `result`) for every such definition, rather than a numbered placeholder per occurrence. That's not an arbitrary choice — Fant's own description treats "the place of resolution's single unnamed source place" as one consistent concept every time this abbreviation is used, so one consistent name for it is the more honest representation, not less.

**That gives us two clean, purely-positional rules, ready to implement without further design discussion:**

1. **Definition has no destinations at all** → synthesize one output port named `result`.
2. **Invocation has an unnamed output slot, and the invoked definition has real destinations** → borrow the positionally-corresponding destination's name for that wire.
3. **What if both — an invocation's unnamed slot points at a definition that *also* has no destinations (rule 1 fired)?** → naturally resolves itself: the invocation just connects to that definition's `result` port, no new logic needed, rules 1 and 2 compose for free.

**What this doesn't resolve, still worth checking tomorrow before assuming it's covered:** whether TAG-146/153's "design file is empty" failures share this same root cause, or are a distinct bug that happened to land in the same issue. That's a five-minute check, not a design question — worth doing first thing before writing the fix, so we don't accidentally patch one thing while leaving the other silently unaddressed.

Good note to end on — this is essentially ready to implement tomorrow with no open design questions left on the main fix, just that one verification step first.
